memo.verdict: Neutral; park; conviction medium. The record parks Liberty Global (LBTYA-US) at $9.45 (2026-09-25) at Triaging. The park rule applies four times over: management at D, business quality at D, predictability at D and trackability at D, and the record does not argue otherwise, because the case's only argument against parking (the parent's cash and Growth assets covering the market capitalisation) bounds the downside without lifting the modal return to the bar. Neutral rather than bearish, because the cover and the dated catalyst make a short or an avoidance-with-prejudice the wrong side of a one-in-three bet with bounded downside; neutral rather than bullish, because the modal path earns about half the 20 percent a year bar (about 11 percent a year over eighteen months and over three years). Conviction medium: fairly sure the modal return is below the bar, fairly sure the downside is bounded near $7.50 to $8.00 a share, unsure at about even odds whether the market will value the telecom equity above zero once separated, which is the whole of the upside. Two named triggers move the recommendation to progress: the price at or below about $8.40 with the calendar intact (the modal path then clears the bar); or two consecutive positive UK broadband quarters without ARPU erosion with the Dutch margin held above 41 percent (the second condition then becomes probable and the case becomes a B-band expected return on the record's branches).
case: The thesis, in the record's words: Liberty Global is a value-crystallisation case, not a growth case; a deal-driven management is dismantling a holding-company structure whose parts the market values above the whole, while the businesses inside the parts decline; at $9.45 the parent's cash and Growth portfolio alone are worth about $13 a share, so a buyer pays less than nothing for half of Virgin Media O2, 90 percent of Ziggo Group and all of Virgin Media Ireland; but that telecom equity is priced at nothing for a reason, and on the modal path the shares return about 11 percent a year against the 20 percent bar.

The change is internal, structural and executed. The group bought out Vodafone's half of VodafoneZiggo for €1.0 billion cash plus a 10 percent stake in the new holding company (closed 2026-07-31; the stake valued at 7.1 times CY2025 EBITDA), is combining it with Telenet into Ziggo Group, separated Telenet from Wyre after the Belgian Competition Authority's approval of 2026-07-23 (Wyre drawing €2.71 billion), cut net corporate costs about 75 percent against 2024 (central EBITDA from about -$200 million in 2024 to about -$50 million targeted for 2026; 40 to 41 percent of corporate headcount removed), sold about $1.2 billion of assets in 2026 to date (UPC Slovakia at €94.8 million net, about 7 times 2025 EBITDA; EdgeConneX fully exited at $726 million total proceeds, 4 times invested capital, more than 30 percent IRR; half the ITV stake), and intends the Ziggo Group spin-off on Euronext Amsterdam as early as mid-2027. Six of the twelve internal forces are strong (perimeter reduction A; strategy B; other leaders B, with van Rooyen as Ziggo Group chief executive, Fruytier as its CFO from September 2026, Melcon as VMO2 CFO from 2026-04-02, Larkin at Liberty Blume from 2026-04-13; standards, acquisitions and balance sheet C), meeting the framework's decision rule with room. The two forces the framework weights most are absent or thin: no chief executive change (Mike Fries since June 2005, Chairman since 2026-01-01) and guidance raised only at the centre. Two red flags are present: dangerous leverage at the operating companies, and a history of debt-funded buybacks (60 percent of shares retired since 2017), now paused. Price rises are F: UK broadband average selling price -4 percent and consumer fixed ARPU -4.6 percent to £46.56 in Q2 2026; the chief executive called the UK a street fight in which retention is prioritised over pricing power.

The external forces run against the assets being crystallised. Of seven, five are headwinds (competition F, disruption D, macro D, supply D, demand D), one mixed (regulation C) and one a mild tailwind on cash only (the company's own capital cycle cresting, C). Competition: Openreach wholesale discounts in zones overlapping the VMO2 footprint, a £50 rebate targeted at VMO2 lines, and copper sales halted where full-fibre coverage exceeds 75 percent; Sky's symmetric 2.5 Gbps and 5 Gbps on CityFibre cut to £35 and £45 a month from £70 and £80; VMO2's 1.1 Gbps tier at £26.99; VMO2 consumer broadband -28,200 in Q2 2026 against a company-compiled consensus of -13,000 and Deutsche Bank's -5,000; postpaid mobile -63,000 after -60,000 in Q1 and -165,000 in Q4 2025; Odido's cuts on 2 Gbps and 8 Gbps tiers forcing VodafoneZiggo onto hollandsnieuwe; KPN holding a 47.8 percent margin while VodafoneZiggo's fell to 41.5 percent. Ofcom proposed on 2026-07-27 to block Openreach's targeted offer (discounts up to £9.50 a month for up to 30 months), which limits one weapon and does not change the direction. Macro: a 10 percent dollar appreciation compresses proportionate EBITDA by 4.8 percent with zero translational coverage; a 10 percent sterling fall cuts EBITDA 6.0 percent and earnings per share 9.0 percent; translation in other comprehensive income -$581 million in H1 2026; swap expiries cluster in 2028 and 2029 and early refinancing of 2030 maturities could add €165 million a year; VMO2's cost of debt 5.3 percent. Supply: 54 percent of voting VodafoneZiggo staff rejected a 2.5 percent rise; Belgian indexation 11 percent; fibre from $5 to $12 to $18 per fibre-kilometre; the Netomnia deal brings £145 million then £120 million of wholesale cost (about 40 then 30 basis points of VMO2 margin). Regulation: the CMA fast-tracked nexfibre's £2.0 billion Netomnia acquisition to Phase 2 on 2026-07-01 with a deadline of 2026-12-15; the Dutch ACM prohibited Glaspoort-Delta Fiber on 2026-06-09; the European Commission is consulting on easing merger guidelines; the Bermuda redomiciliation of November 2023 lets spin-offs pass by simple majority.
counter_case: At Building Block 1, the bull case at its strongest (Deutsche Bank, Buy, $23.00 target, 2026-07-24; the chief executive's $37 to $40 a share value-unlock ambition on the Q2 2026 call): cash of about $2.0 billion and Growth assets of about $2.9 billion are worth about $13 a share against a $9.45 price, so the telecom equity (half of VMO2, 90 percent of Ziggo Group, all of Virgin Media Ireland) is in the price for less than nothing; the Sunrise spin-off of November 2024 shows the mechanism, Sunrise having represented 20 percent of proportionate EBITDA and captured 45 percent of the combined market capitalisation; the Ziggo Group spin-off is dated, funded without external capital and pulled forward; management has met every cash target for four years and has sold every asset it said it would at or above its marks; the price is at a 52-week low with relative strength at the 7th percentile, which is where a corporate-change case is bought. The record concedes the cover at the preferred mark, the mechanism as precedented, the calendar, the competence at transactions, and that the modal downside is bounded in a way a growth case's is not. It does not concede that the telecom equity is worth much more than nothing today: VMO2 at 5.89 times net total debt to EBITDA including vendor financing against a 4.0 to 5.0 times target; VodafoneZiggo near 6.0 times at end-2025; Ziggo Group's 2026 free cash flow base of about €120 million against a 2028 target of €500 million the sell-side calls extremely challenging; the Sunrise precedent a listing at 4.5 times leverage funded by a Liberty cash injection and Swiss refinancing below 3 percent, of an operator that then fell 13 percent in a year on weak guidance; Ziggo Group starting near 6.0 times into a Dutch market whose regulator has just blocked a fibre deal and whose staff have just rejected a pay offer, with a €65 million a year Vodafone brand fee. An equity slice this thin on a declining EBITDA is an option, the market prices it as one, and the two quarters since the catalysts were pulled forward have shown the market marking the option down as the operating data worsened; a spin-off changes who holds the option, not what it is worth, unless the operating data turn. The framework rates the modal path (about 11 percent a year, half the bar), not the bounded downside; the bar-clearing path needs two conditions and sits at about one chance in three; and the people making the case have not bought a share on the open market in twelve months. Where the bull case would win: VodafoneZiggo's margin stabilising above 41 percent for two quarters and the first Benelux disposal at or above book, at which the second condition becomes probable and the case moves to a B-band expected return.

At Building Block 2: the foundations are stronger than the outputs show, because last-mile cable and fibre are irreplaceable on competitors' own view, fixed-mobile convergence halves churn in the Netherlands, network-company structures let Liberty capture private fibre multiples of about 18 times against 5.9 times for integrated peers, and management has delivered every cash target for four years. The record concedes the assets and the arithmetic of the arbitrage, and answers that a moat being overbuilt by three networks in 80 percent of one footprint is a moat in name; that convergence at VMO2 is 40.7 percent against 71 to 72 percent at KPN and Proximus, so the defensive tool is least deployed where most needed; that the 18 times multiples belong to InfraVia (50 percent of nexfibre) and Fluvius (33.2 percent of Wyre), not to Liberty's equity; and that the cash targets were met while retail revenue, ARPU and free cash flow fell.
triggers: - To progress: the price at or below about $8.40 with the calendar intact (the modal path clears the 20 percent bar over eighteen months; over three years the entry price is $7.50); or two consecutive positive VMO2 consumer broadband quarters without ARPU erosion with the VodafoneZiggo margin held above 41 percent.

- Condition one, the spin-off completing by end-2027 (probable, about 65 percent): what would change the view is no disposal announced by Q1 2027 (Alarm), or a listing document that pushes the date beyond 2027 (Invalidate).

- Condition two, the market valuing the telecom equity above zero once separated (plausible, about 55 percent conditional on the first): what would raise it is VodafoneZiggo's margin stabilising above 41 percent for two quarters and the first Benelux disposal at or above book.

- Condition three, the UK stabilising before the overbuild and the wholesale costs take the margin (unlikely within eighteen months, about 30 percent): confirm on two consecutive positive broadband quarters without ARPU erosion; Alarm at VMO2 losses above 20,000 a quarter or ARPU below £45; Invalidate at losses above 30,000 a quarter for two quarters, or a VodafoneZiggo margin below 40 percent.

- Condition four, the 2028 to 2029 refinancing wall and the dollar leaving the equity intact: Alarm at S&P moving from negative outlook to a downgrade; Invalidate at a swap life below two years without replacement; a 10 percent dollar rise takes 4.8 percent off proportionate EBITDA; under the worse drop-through FY2028 earnings per share about -1.51 USD and free cash flow about $30 million.

- Deleveraging: Alarm at parent cash below $1.5 billion (the research's warning below $1.2 billion) or no disposal announced by Q1 2027; Invalidate at a distribution suspension at VMO2 or a covenant breach; VMO2 leverage 5.89 times against the 4.0 to 5.0 times corridor; Ziggo Group toward 4.5 times by 2028 via €1.2 to €1.4 billion of property and tower disposals.
